key_insight: AI agents systematically overestimate their chance of success: some agents that succeed only 22% of the time predict 77% success. Surprisingly, probability estimates given before execution—despite having less information—can discriminate success better than standard post-execution self-reports.
problem_solved: Quantifies and exposes 'agentic uncertainty'—the mismatch between agents' self-assessed success probabilities and their actual success—revealing pervasive overconfidence and testing when pre-, during-, and post-execution estimates are most informative.
method: Elicit success-probability estimates from agents at three phases: before, during, and after task execution.
Compare predicted probabilities to actual outcomes using calibration and discrimination metrics to quantify overconfidence and predictive power.
Analyze phase-wise differences (pre vs during vs post) and report aggregate examples showing extreme overconfidence (e.g., 77% predicted vs 22% actual).
impact: Highlights a practical reliability gap: agents' confidence is often misleading, which matters for deployment, monitoring, and human–AI handoff policies. Practitioners should treat agent self-assessments with skepticism and prefer calibrated uncertainty estimates when possible.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing predicted vs actual success rates for representative agents (e.g., 77% vs 22%).
Timeline diagram showing the three elicitation phases (pre / during / post) with associated calibration and discrimination scores.
Reliability (calibration) curve and Brier score snapshot to show overconfidence and miscalibration.
Icon set: warning/uncertainty symbol, gauge for confidence, and checklist for actionable monitoring steps.
paper_authors: Jean Kaddour, Srijan Patel, Gbètondji Dovonon, Leo Richter, Pasquale Minervini
